title: Unit 6 test: Energy and Momentum of Rotating Systems
author: cm-5
directions: Unit 6 test on the energy and momentum of rotating systems, 70 minutes. Spend 25 minutes on Section I (12 multiple-choice questions) and 45 minutes on Section II (2 free-response questions). Any calculator is allowed. Use g = 9.8 m/s^2 and SI units; give angular positions and speeds in radians, and state the sense of rotation you take as positive. Raw points totalled with the key are a practice measure, not an AP® score.

parts.directions: Mark one answer for each question. Neglect air resistance and axle friction unless a question includes them.

items.prompt: A uniform solid sphere and a thin spherical shell have the same mass and radius and spin about axes through their centers at the same angular speed. What is the ratio K_shell/K_solid of their kinetic energies?
items.rationale: K = ½Iω^2 at the same ω, so the ratio is I_shell/I_solid = (2/3)MR^2/((2/5)MR^2) = 5/3.

distractorNotes.A: This inverts the ratio of rotational inertias.
distractorNotes.B: This assumes equal mass and radius give equal kinetic energy, ignoring how the mass is distributed.
distractorNotes.D: This compares a hoop (I = MR^2) with the solid sphere instead of a spherical shell.

items.prompt: A uniform 0.50 kg rod 0.60 m long rotates at 10 rad/s about a fixed axis through one end, perpendicular to the rod. What is its kinetic energy?

distractorNotes.A: This uses I = ML^2/12, the rotational inertia about the center, not the end.
distractorNotes.C: This is ½Mv^2 for the center's speed of 3.0 m/s, as if the whole rod moved at that speed.
distractorNotes.D: This is ½Mv^2 for the free end's speed of 6.0 m/s, as if every part moved that fast.

items.prompt: The net torque on a wheel depends on its angle of rotation as τ = 2.0θ, in N·m with θ in radians. How much work does this torque do as the wheel turns from θ = 0 to θ = 3.0 rad?
items.rationale: W = ∫τ dθ from 0 to 3.0 = [θ^2] from 0 to 3.0 = 9.0 J, the triangular area under the τ–θ graph.

distractorNotes.A: This is dτ/dθ, a derivative, instead of the integral of τ.
distractorNotes.B: This is the torque at 3.0 rad, in N·m, not a work.
distractorNotes.C: This multiplies the final torque by the whole angle, as if the torque were 6.0 N·m throughout.

items.prompt: A motor turns a drum at a steady 2.0 revolutions per second while exerting a torque of 15 N·m on it. What power does the motor deliver?
items.rationale: P = τω with ω = (2.0 rev/s)(2π rad/rev) = 12.6 rad/s, so P = (15)(12.6) = 1.9 × 10^2 W.

distractorNotes.B: This multiplies the torque by the rate in rev/s without converting to rad/s.
distractorNotes.C: This converts with π instead of 2π radians per revolution.
distractorNotes.D: This divides the torque by the rate instead of multiplying.

items.prompt: A wheel (I = 0.30 kg·m^2) spins counterclockwise at 2.0 rad/s. A constant counterclockwise torque of 0.40 N·m then acts on it for 3.0 s. What is its angular speed afterward?
items.rationale: The angular impulse τΔt = (0.40)(3.0) = 1.2 N·m·s raises L from (0.30)(2.0) = 0.60 to 1.8 kg·m^2/s, so ω = 1.8/0.30 = 6.0 rad/s.

distractorNotes.A: This reads the angular impulse, 1.2 N·m·s, as the angular speed.
distractorNotes.B: This assumes a steady torque only keeps a spinning wheel turning at the same rate.
distractorNotes.C: This is the change in angular speed only, leaving out the initial 2.0 rad/s.

items.prompt: A 2.0 kg puck slides at a constant 3.0 m/s in the +x direction along the line y = 4.0 m. What is the magnitude of its angular momentum about the origin when it is at x = 3.0 m?
items.rationale: L = mvr⊥, where r⊥ is the perpendicular distance from the origin to the line of motion, 4.0 m: L = (2.0)(3.0)(4.0) = 24 kg·m^2/s, the same at every point of the line.

distractorNotes.A: This uses the x-coordinate, 3.0 m, as the moment arm.
distractorNotes.C: This multiplies by the full distance r = 5.0 m instead of the moment arm.
distractorNotes.D: This assumes straight-line motion has no angular momentum.

items.prompt: A space probe spinning freely at 0.50 rev/s extends two long booms, which raises its rotational inertia from 400 kg·m^2 to 1000 kg·m^2. What is its new rate of spin?
items.rationale: No external torque acts, so I_1ω_1 = I_2ω_2: ω_2 = (400/1000)(0.50 rev/s) = 0.20 rev/s.

distractorNotes.B: This scales by √(400/1000), as if rotational kinetic energy were conserved.
distractorNotes.C: This multiplies by 1000/400, inverting the ratio.
distractorNotes.D: This assumes the spin rate cannot change without an external torque.

items.prompt: A beetle walks from the rim of a freely turning horizontal disk to its center. How do the disk's angular speed and the beetle–disk system's kinetic energy change?
items.rationale: Angular momentum is conserved and I decreases, so ω increases; K = L^2/(2I) increases because the beetle does positive work pulling itself inward.

distractorNotes.A: Kinetic energy is not conserved when I changes at constant L.
distractorNotes.B: With I smaller and L constant, ω must change.
distractorNotes.C: Moving mass inward lowers I, which raises ω.

items.prompt: A thin-walled pipe (a hoop) rolls without slipping from rest down a ramp, dropping a height of 0.80 m. What is its speed at the bottom?
items.rationale: For a hoop, K = ½Mv^2 + ½(MR^2)(v/R)^2 = Mv^2, so Mgh = Mv^2 and v = √(gh) = √((9.8)(0.80)) = 2.8 m/s.

distractorNotes.B: This uses the solid-cylinder result, v = √(4gh/3).
distractorNotes.C: This uses the solid-sphere result, v = √(10gh/7).
distractorNotes.D: This ignores rotation: v = √(2gh) for sliding without friction.

items.prompt: A uniform solid sphere rolls without slipping. What fraction of its total kinetic energy is rotational?

distractorNotes.A: This is the ratio I/(MR^2), not the fraction of the energy.
distractorNotes.D: This is the fraction for a hoop, whose two parts are equal.

items.prompt: A satellite in a circular orbit of radius r around a planet has period T. What would the period be for a circular orbit of the same radius around a planet with four times the mass?
items.rationale: T^2 = 4π^2r^3/(GM), so T ∝ 1/√M at fixed r: four times the mass halves the period.

distractorNotes.A: This makes T inversely proportional to M rather than to √M.
distractorNotes.B: This has the dependence on mass backward.
distractorNotes.C: This assumes the period depends only on the radius.

items.prompt: A satellite on an elliptical orbit around a planet passes its closest point, 2.0 × 10^7 m from the planet's center, at 6.0 × 10^3 m/s. Its farthest point is 5.0 × 10^7 m from the center. What is its speed there?
items.rationale: At both ends the velocity is perpendicular to the radius, and angular momentum is conserved: v_a = v_pr_p/r_a = (6.0 × 10^3)(2.0/5.0) = 2.4 × 10^3 m/s.

distractorNotes.A: This multiplies by r_a/r_p, so the satellite would be faster when farther away.
distractorNotes.B: This scales the speed by √(r_p/r_a), the rule for circular orbits of different radii.

parts.directions: Show your work and units; points are awarded for reasoning as well as answers. Allow about 20 minutes for Question 1 (10 points) and 25 minutes for Question 2 (10 points). Question 2 is a paper investigation with supplied, invented data; such investigations do not replace the hands-on laboratory work the course framework calls for, and they do not count toward the AP Course Audit or college lab credit.

items.prompt: A flywheel is a uniform solid disk of mass 8.0 kg and radius 0.30 m on a frictionless axle. Starting from rest at t = 0, a motor applies a torque τ(t) = 6.0 − 1.5t, in N·m with t in seconds, for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4.0 s, and is then disconnected.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Find the flywheel's angular momentum and angular speed at t = 4.0 s.

rubric.criterion: Integrates the torque: L = ∫ from 0 to 4.0 of (6.0 − 1.5t) dt = 6.0t − 0.75t^2 = 12 kg·m^2/s.
Uses I = ½MR^2 = 0.36 kg·m^2 to get ω = 33 rad/s (accept 33–34 rad/s).

steps: Angular impulse equals ΔL: ∫τ dt = [6.0t − 0.75t^2] from 0 to 4.0 = 24 − 12 = 12 kg·m^2/s.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find the power the motor delivers at t = 2.0 s.

rubric.criterion: Uses P = τω with τ(2.0) = 3.0 N·m to get P = 75 W.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Find the total work done by the motor from t = 0 to t = 4.0 s.

rubric.criterion: Uses the work–energy theorem: W = ½Iω^2 (or integrates P = τω over time).
Gets W = 2.0 × 10^2 J (accept 195–205 J).

steps: The motor's torque is the only torque, so W = ΔK = ½(0.36)(33.3)^2.
W = 200 J; integrating P dt gives the same, since ∫τω dt = L^2/(2I) = 144/0.72 = 200 J.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: After the motor is disconnected, the flywheel is pressed against a second disk, with rotational inertia 0.12 kg·m^2, initially at rest on the same axle, until they turn together. Find their common angular speed and the kinetic energy converted to internal energy.

rubric.criterion: Conserves angular momentum: 12 kg·m^2/s = (0.36 + 0.12)ω.
Gets ω = 25 rad/s.
Finds K after = ½(0.48)(25)^2 = 150 J, so 50 J is converted (accept 48–52 J).

steps: K drops from 200 J to 150 J.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Explain why angular momentum, but not kinetic energy, is conserved when the disks are pressed together.

rubric.criterion: States that the torques the disks exert on each other are internal (equal and opposite) and the axle exerts no torque, so the total L is unchanged, while the friction between the slipping surfaces converts kinetic energy to internal energy.

parts.answer: The frictional torques between the disks are an internal third-law pair and the axle is frictionless, so the net external torque is zero and L is conserved; the surfaces slip while the friction acts, so kinetic energy is lost to internal energy.
steps: Internal torques cancel in the total.
Kinetic friction between slipping surfaces does net negative work on the pair.

items.prompt:
The data below are invented for a paper investigation, which does not replace the hands-on laboratory work the course framework calls for and does not count toward the AP Course Audit or college lab credit. A student wants to find the rotational inertia I of a bicycle wheel that turns on a fixed horizontal axle, as shown. Neglect friction in the axle bearings and air resistance. A felt pad held in a spring clamp can be lowered onto the rim, where it exerts a friction torque τ_f that she assumes is constant. To measure τ_f, she lowers the pad and pulls the rim around slowly at a steady rate with a spring scale held tangent to the rim, 0.31 m from the axle; the scale reads 0.48 N. In each trial she then spins the wheel with the pad raised, reads its angular speed ω_0 from a rotation sensor on the axle, lowers the pad at once and records the number of revolutions n the wheel turns before it stops.
| Trial | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ω_0 (rad/s) | 8.0 | 12.0 | 16.0 | 20.0 | 24.0 |
| n (revolutions) | 3.9 | 8.4 | 15.1 | 23.4 | 34.0 |

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe how the student should carry out the spin-down trials so that every trial has the same braking torque and n is measured accurately. Include one way to reduce random uncertainty.

rubric.criterion: Applies the pad the same way in every trial (same clamp setting and spring compression, same place on the rim, pad clean and allowed to cool between trials) and counts from the moment the pad touches the rim.
Measures n with the rotation sensor (or by counting a marked spoke passing a fixed pointer, including the last fraction of a turn) and repeats each ω_0 several times, averaging n.

parts.answer: Sample: set the clamp once and never adjust it, so the pad presses equally hard each time; wipe the pad and let it cool between runs; lower the pad as soon as ω_0 is read and count revolutions from that moment until the wheel stops, using the rotation sensor's angle (or a chalk mark on one spoke and a fixed pointer, estimating the final fraction of a turn); repeat each starting speed three times and average n.
steps: The model needs the same constant torque in every trial, so the pad's pressure and condition must not change.
Repeating trials and averaging reduces random error in n.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Use the rotational work–energy theorem to show that n = [I/(4πτ_f)]ω_0^2 if τ_f is constant, and state what the student should graph to obtain a straight line.

rubric.criterion: Writes −τ_f(2πn) = 0 − ½Iω_0^2: the brake's negative work through the angle 2πn radians equals the loss of rotational kinetic energy.
Rearranges to n = [I/(4πτ_f)]ω_0^2 and states the graph: n on the vertical axis against ω_0^2, a straight line through the origin with slope I/(4πτ_f).

parts.answer: W = −τ_fΔθ with Δθ = 2πn rad, and W = ΔK = −½Iω_0^2, so 2πnτ_f = ½Iω_0^2 and n = [I/(4πτ_f)]ω_0^2. Plot n against ω_0^2: a line through the origin with slope I/(4πτ_f).
steps: The pad's torque is the only torque that does work while the wheel stops; bearing friction and air resistance are negligible.
Divide both sides by 4πτ_f; n is proportional to ω_0^2.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate ω_0^2 for each trial, plot n against ω_0^2 on the grid provided, and draw a best-fit line.

rubric.criterion: Computes ω_0^2 = 64, 144, 256, 400 and 576 rad^2/s^2 and plots the five points on labeled, scaled axes.
Draws one straight best-fit line through the points, passing close to the origin.

parts.answer: Points (64, 3.9), (144, 8.4), (256, 15.1), (400, 23.4) and (576, 34.0) lie close to a straight line through the origin.
steps: For example, trial 3: (16.0 rad/s)^2 = 256 rad^2/s^2.
Start both axes at zero so the intercept can be seen.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Find τ_f from the spring-scale reading, explaining why the steady pull gives it, and use your line to find I.

rubric.criterion: The rim turns at a steady rate, so the net torque is zero and the friction torque balances the scale's: τ_f = FR = (0.48 N)(0.31 m) = 0.149 N·m (accept 0.14–0.15 N·m).
Finds a slope of about 0.059 revolution per (rad/s)^2, that is 0.059 s^2 (accept 0.056–0.062), and I = 4πτ_f × slope = 0.11 kg·m^2 (accept 0.10–0.12 kg·m^2).

steps: Zero angular acceleration means zero net torque; the scale's torque is FR with the force tangent to the rim. With bearing friction and air resistance negligible, the pull balances the pad's friction torque τ_f.
A least-squares fit gives slope 0.0588 s^2 and intercept 0.02 revolution, close to zero as the model requires; I = 4π(0.1488)(0.0588) = 0.110 kg·m^2.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: The spring-scale test was done with the wheel turning slowly, but the trials begin at much higher speeds. Suppose the pad's friction torque is about 10% smaller at the speeds of the trials than in the test. Would the student's value of I be too large or too small, and by roughly what fraction? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Too large, by about 11% (a factor 1/0.9).
Explains that a smaller real torque, 0.9τ_f, lets the wheel turn more revolutions, so the slope is I/(4π × 0.9τ_f); multiplying that slope by 4π times the larger test value τ_f gives I/0.9.

parts.answer: Too large by about 11%: during the trials the torque is 0.9τ_f, so the wheel turns farther and the slope is I/(4π(0.9τ_f)); the student multiplies it by 4πτ_f and gets I/0.9 ≈ 1.11I.
steps: n = Iω_0^2/(4πτ_real) with τ_real = 0.9τ_f.
I_found = 4πτ_f × slope = I(τ_f/τ_real) = I/0.9.
